before: What made Azusa Street astonishing to its visitors was the mixing of races. In the United States of that time, the law and the custom of many places kept Black and white people apart, in schools, trains, neighborhoods and most churches. Yet people of different races knelt at the same altar at Azusa Street, prayed for one another, and heard preachers of different races. *The Apostolic Faith* reported this with wonder. Frank Bartleman, a white Holiness writer who was at the mission, also described how the divisions between the races seemed to fall away in the meetings.

before: Historians do not all agree on how far this unity went. Some have emphasized the interracial worship and called it one of the great achievements of the movement. Others point out that the unity did not last, that it existed within a society that was still segregated, and that even at Azusa Street the leadership and the experience of Black and white worshipers were not always the same. Some also say the early reports, written by believers who were excited about what they saw, may make the unity sound more complete than it was.

before: When Parham visited Azusa Street in late 1906, he was displeased. He objected to the mixing of the races in worship, and he also disliked some of the manner of the meetings. He and Seymour parted. Parham's teaching on the Spirit had shaped the early movement, yet he held racist views that were contrary to the gospel. Here our tradition must speak plainly. A man may be used by God in one part of his life and still be wrong in another. The gift of tongues does not remove prejudice. Only repentance and the love of Christ do that.

before: **The Church of God in Christ.** Charles Harrison Mason, an African American Holiness leader, led the Church of God in Christ. He visited Azusa Street in 1907 and was baptized in the Holy Spirit. The Church of God in Christ then became a Pentecostal body, and today it is one of the largest African American denominations in the United States. In the early years Mason ordained and gave credentials to white ministers, because the new Pentecostal groups did not yet have their own organizations.

**The Assemblies of God.** In 1914, in Hot Springs, Arkansas, many of those white ministers met and formed the Assemblies of God. Their reasons were varied. They wanted a way to support missionaries, order their churches and protect their doctrine, and historians note that the effect was that white and Black Pentecostals were organized in separate bodies. Many white Pentecostal groups were formed in this way. The separation was not the fruit of the Spirit. It was a wound.

**A white fellowship, and a repentance.** In 1948, white Pentecostal denominations formed the Pentecostal Fellowship of North America, which did not include the Black Pentecostal bodies. In 1994, in Memphis, Tennessee, leaders met and the white fellowship was dissolved. In its place a new group was formed, the Pentecostal and Charismatic Churches of North America, with white and Black leadership. White leaders acknowledged and repented of the racism that had been present in the movement. The meeting is often called the Memphis Miracle, and it shows that the story does not end in failure. When God's people confess their sin, He forgives and restores.
